s: In which year were Agenda 2030 and the Sustainable Development Goals adopted?
x: The MDGs began in 2000, WSSD was in 2002, Rio+20 in 2012 and Agenda 2030 was adopted in 2015.

s: The Millennium Declaration provided the framework for which of the following?
x: The Millennium Declaration set up the MDGs; Agenda 21 is the action plan and 'The Future We Want' came from Rio+20 in 2012.

s: Arrange in chronological order: 1. Our Common Future 2. Johannesburg Declaration 3. Stockholm Declaration 4. Rio Declaration
x: Stockholm Declaration 1972, Our Common Future 1987, Rio Declaration 1992, Johannesburg Declaration 2002.

s: The first World Conference on Environment was held at which place and in which year?
x: The first world conference on the environment was held at Stockholm in 1972 (UNCHE). Rio (1992) was the Earth Summit and Johannesburg (2002) Rio+10.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about UNEP?
o: Its headquarters is in Nairobi, Kenya.
It focuses on global environmental coordination.
It originated from the Rio Earth Summit, 1992.
x: UNEP came out of the 1972 Stockholm Conference, not the 1992 Rio summit. It is headquartered in Nairobi.

s: In which year was the Kyoto conference on climate change held?
x: Stockholm was 1972, Rio 1992, Kyoto 1997 (climate change) and Johannesburg 2002 (sustainable development).

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
x: Rio+5 was held in New York (1997); Rio+10 was in Johannesburg (2002) and Rio+20 in Rio de Janeiro (2012).

s: What was the formal name of the 2002 Johannesburg summit (Rio+10)?
o: UN Conference on Environment and Development
x: Rio+10 was the World Summit on Sustainable Development (WSSD); UNCSD was Rio+20 in 2012.

s: 'The Future We Want' was the outcome document of which conference?
o: UN Conference on Environment and Development, 1992
UN Conference on the Human Environment, 1972
x: 'The Future We Want' came out of Rio+20, the UN Conference on Sustainable Development (2012), not Rio 1992.

s: What is the main task of the UN Commission on Sustainable Development (CSD)?
o: Reviewing implementation of Agenda 21 and the Rio Declaration
x: The CSD reviews how far Agenda 21 and the Rio Declaration have been implemented.

s: At which conference was the decision taken to frame the Sustainable Development Goals?
x: The SDGs were born at Rio+20 (2012) and adopted in the 2030 Agenda in 2015.

s: Where was 'Transforming our World: the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development' adopted in September 2015?
x: The 2030 Agenda was adopted at the UN Sustainable Development Summit (UNGA 70th session) in New York on 25 September 2015.

s: Which of the following is NOT one of the five UN agencies of the Partnership for Action on Green Economy (PAGE)?
x: PAGE brings together UNEP, UNDP, ILO, UNIDO and UNITAR; the WTO is not a member.

s: Which period did the Millennium Development Goals, which preceded the SDGs, cover?
x: The MDGs ran from 2000 to 2015, followed by the SDGs from 2016.

s: Gro Harlem Brundtland, who chaired the commission that produced 'Our Common Future', was then Prime Minister of which country?
x: Gro Harlem Brundtland was Prime Minister of Norway when she chaired the WCED.

s: By what formal name is the Brundtland Commission known?
o: World Commission on Environment and Development
UN Conference on the Human Environment
x: The Brundtland Commission is the World Commission on Environment and Development (WCED), which published Our Common Future in 1987.

s: Which of the following is the Brundtland Report's definition of sustainable development?
o: Development that maximises economic growth using all available resources
Development that protects the environment by halting industrial growth
Development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs
Development that meets the needs of developed countries first
x: Our Common Future (1987) defined sustainable development as meeting present needs without compromising future generations.

s: In which year was Our Common Future (the Brundtland Report) published?
x: The order is Stockholm Declaration 1972, Our Common Future 1987, Rio Declaration 1992 and Johannesburg Declaration 2002.

s: What does the principle of Common but Differentiated Responsibilities (CBDR) imply?
o: Responsibilities are shared, but developed nations carry greater duties
Only developing countries bear responsibility for environmental protection
All countries have identical environmental duties and identical capacities
Environmental duties are restricted to countries that caused no historical pollution
x: CBDR recognises shared responsibility while assigning greater duties to developed nations in view of their capacities and historical contribution.

s: Which principle says that lack of full scientific certainty is no reason to postpone cost-effective measures against environmental harm?
x: This is the precautionary principle; it does not allow preventive action to be postponed until full certainty.

s: Which of the following runs counter to sustainable development?
o: Maximising economic growth at any cost
x: Maximising growth at any cost conflicts with sustainable development, which balances economic, social and environmental concerns.

s: What does the principle of carrying capacity in sustainable development mean?
o: The polluter bears the cost of pollution control
Human use must stay within what ecosystems can support
x: Carrying capacity means using resources within what ecosystems can support; the other options describe CBDR, polluter pays and precaution.

s: Which principle of sustainable development holds that the present generation must not deplete resources at the cost of future generations?
x: Intergenerational equity is the heart of the Brundtland definition: today's users hold resources in trust for future users.

s: Which principle of sustainable development makes the polluter bear the cost of preventing and controlling pollution?
x: Under the polluter pays principle, the cost falls on the polluter, not on the public.

s: Which of the following is consistent with the scope of sustainable development?
o: Running down natural capital to maximise current output
Excluding disadvantaged groups from development planning
Treating environmental protection and development as mutually exclusive
Meeting present needs while promoting equity within and across generations
x: Sustainable development includes meeting present needs, equity within and across generations, and inclusion. It rejects depletion of natural capital and the opposition of environment to development.

s: Which of the following is excluded from the scope of sustainable development?
o: Growth that runs down natural capital
x: Sustainable development includes present needs, equity and inclusion, but excludes growth that runs down natural capital.

s: How many goals and targets does 'Transforming our World: the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development' contain?
x: The 2030 Agenda contains 17 Sustainable Development Goals and 169 targets. It is also associated with 232 indicators.

s: From which year did the Sustainable Development Goals formally come into force?
x: The 2030 Agenda and its SDGs were adopted in 2015 and came into force from 2016.

s: What was India's rank in the SDG Index of the Sustainable Development Report 2025?
x: India ranked 99th out of 167 in SDR 2025, entering the top 100 for the first time.

s: How many indicators are there for the 17 Sustainable Development Goals?
x: The SDGs have 17 goals, 169 targets and 232 indicators.

s: Which country was ranked first in the Sustainable Development Report 2026?
x: Finland topped SDR 2026, in which India reached its best-ever rank of 94th.

s: In Andhra Pradesh, Sustainable Development Goal targets have been built into which vision document?
x: SDG targets have been built into Swarna Andhra @2047, Andhra Pradesh's long-term vision.

s: The Rio Declaration adopted at the 1992 Earth Summit contained how many principles?
x: The Rio Declaration contains 27 principles relating to environment and development.

s: Which of the following was an outcome of the 1992 UN Conference on Environment and Development?
x: The CBD, Agenda 21, the Rio Declaration and the UNFCCC came from Rio 1992; The Future We Want was the Rio+20 (2012) outcome.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct?
o: Agenda 21 is a comprehensive action plan for the 21st century
Our Common Future defined sustainable development
The Rio Declaration sets out 27 principles on environment and development
The Forest Principles are a legally binding treaty on forests
x: The Forest Principles are a non-binding statement on the sustainable management of forests.

s: Which of the following is NOT one of the three classic pillars of sustainable development?
x: The three classic pillars are economic development, social equity and environmental protection. Military security is not one of them.

s: In business terms, what does the triple bottom line of sustainable development stand for?
x: The triple bottom line is commonly expressed as People, Planet and Profit, corresponding broadly to social, environmental and economic concerns.

s:
Assertion (A): Economic sustainability does not mean maximising profits without considering social or environmental impacts.
Reason (R): Sustainable development seeks a balance between economic growth, social equity and environmental protection.
o: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
x: Both are true, and the balance in R is the reason economic sustainability cannot ignore social and environmental impacts.

s: For which body was 'The Limits to Growth' (1972) prepared?
x: The Limits to Growth was a report for the Club of Rome by an MIT team including Donella and Dennis Meadows.

s: Who launched the World Conservation Strategy of 1980?
x: The World Conservation Strategy (1980) was launched by IUCN with UNEP and WWF.

s: Who among the following were associated with 'The Limits to Growth' (1972), prepared for the Club of Rome?
x: The Limits to Growth was written by an MIT team including Donella and Dennis Meadows for the Club of Rome.

s:
Consider the following statements about 'The Limits to Growth':
1. It was prepared for the Club of Rome in 1972.
2. It used a computer model to argue that growth cannot go on forever on finite resources.
3. It gave the first definition of sustainable development.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: The Limits to Growth (1972, Club of Rome, MIT team) used a computer model; the first definition of SD came from the Brundtland Report, 1987.

s: How is Green GDP obtained?
o: Adding only gross industrial output to conventional GDP
Subtracting unpaid household work from GDP
Adjusting GDP for natural-resource depletion and environmental damage
Measuring only the value of protected forests
x: Green GDP adjusts conventional GDP to account for natural-resource depletion and environmental damage.

s: Which measure of sustainability adds unpaid work and subtracts pollution, crime and resource loss?
x: The Genuine Progress Indicator makes these adjustments; Earth Overshoot Day marks when humanity's demand exceeds what Earth can regenerate that year.

s: What does the ecological footprint of a population refer to?
o: Annual date on which its natural resources are exhausted
Amount of carbon dioxide emitted by its industries alone
Productive land and sea needed to meet its consumption and absorb its wastes
Total number of endangered species in its territory
x: An ecological footprint estimates the productive land and sea area required to supply consumption and absorb generated wastes, expressed in global hectares.

s: Who conceived Earth Overshoot Day?
x: Earth Overshoot Day was conceived by Andrew Simms of the New Economics Foundation, UK; the first campaign was in 2006.

s: In which unit is the ecological footprint measured?
x: The ecological footprint is the productive land and sea needed to meet consumption and absorb wastes, measured in global hectares.

s: With which organisation did the first Earth Overshoot Day campaign of 2006 begin?
x: Earth Overshoot Day was conceived by Andrew Simms; its first campaign in 2006 was with the Global Footprint Network.

s: The National Green Tribunal is required to apply which combination of principles while adjudicating environmental cases?
o: Sustainable development, precautionary principle and polluter-pays principle
Public trust doctrine, absolute liability and eminent domain
Common but differentiated responsibilities, prior appropriation and res judicata
Inter-generational equity, federal supremacy and parliamentary privilege
x: The NGT must apply the principles of sustainable development, precautionary action and polluter pays.

s: How does the National Environment Policy, 2006 treat conservation and livelihood security?
o: Objectives relevant only to urban areas
x: The National Environment Policy, 2006 holds that conservation and livelihood security are linked rather than opposed.

s: The Wetlands (Conservation & Management) Rules, 2010 were framed on the recommendation of an Expert Panel under which policy?
o: National Action Plan on Climate Change, 2008
x: An Expert Panel constituted under the National Environment Policy, 2006 led to the Wetlands Rules, 2010.

s: At which of the following places does the National Green Tribunal NOT have a bench?
x: NGT benches are at Bhopal, Pune, Kolkata and Chennai, not Hyderabad.

s: Which landmark judgment recognised sustainable development, the precautionary principle and the polluter-pays principle as part of Indian environmental law?
o: Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action v. Union of India
Vellore Citizens' Welfare Forum v. Union of India
Narmada Bachao Andolan v. Union of India
x: Vellore Citizens' Welfare Forum v. Union of India (1996) recognised sustainable development, the precautionary principle and the polluter-pays principle in Indian environmental law.

s: Which case is associated with the polluter-pays principle in India, alongside the Vellore Citizens' Welfare Forum case?
o: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
S.R. Bommai v. Union of India
Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
M.C. Mehta v. Union of India
x: M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1996) applied the polluter-pays principle.

s: In which year was the Vellore Citizens' Welfare Forum v. Union of India judgment delivered?
x: The Vellore Citizens' Welfare Forum case was decided in 1996.

s: Where is the headquarters (principal bench) of the National Green Tribunal?
x: NGT is headquartered in New Delhi, with benches at Bhopal, Pune, Kolkata and Chennai.

s: Which set of measures is associated with the Sustainability and Climate Resilience pillar of Swarna Andhra @2047?
o: Renewable energy, green mobility and sustainable urban planning
Coal expansion, private transport and dispersed urbanisation
Nuclear energy, rural depopulation and industrial zoning
River diversion, road widening and conventional urban planning
x: The pillar includes renewable energy, green mobility and sustainable urban planning.

s: Under the Swarna Andhra @2047 vision, to what level is the share of renewable energy targeted to rise by 2047?
x: Renewable energy contributes about 30% now, with a target of more than 75% by 2047.

s: With which national vision is the Swarna Andhra @2047 vision aligned?
x: Swarna Andhra @2047 is aligned with Viksit Bharat @2047, not Atmanirbhar Bharat @2035.

s: Swarna Andhra @2047 is organised around how many 'Sutras'?
x: Swarna Andhra @2047 has Ten Sutras, aiming at a Wealthy, Healthy and Happy Andhra Pradesh.

s: Swarna Andhra @2047 aims at which kind of Andhra Pradesh by 2047?
x: Swarna Andhra @2047 aims at a 'Wealthy, Healthy and Happy' AP, aligned with Viksit Bharat @2047.

s: How many targets do the 17 Sustainable Development Goals have?
x: The 17 SDGs carry 169 targets; 196 is the usual trap.

s: Which group of SDGs extends the concerns of the Millennium Development Goals?
x: Goals 1-7 extend MDG concerns; Goals 8-10 cover jobs, infrastructure and distribution, and the last seven focus on sustainability.

s: SDG 10 (Reduced Inequalities) aims to bring remittance costs below what level?
x: The SDG 10 remittance-cost target is below 3%, not 5%.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
x: Clean Water and Sanitation is SDG 6. No Poverty is Goal 1, Climate Action Goal 13 and Partnerships Goal 17.

s: What does SDG 12 relate to?
x: SDG 12 is Responsible Consumption and Production; SDG 4 is education, SDG 7 energy and SDG 16 peace and justice.

s: Which of the following is SDG 14?
x: SDG 14 is Life Below Water; SDG 15 is Life on Land, SDG 11 Sustainable Cities and SDG 12 Responsible Consumption.

s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
x: SDG 10 is Reduced Inequalities. Goal 4 is Quality Education, Goal 5 is Gender Equality and Goal 13 is Climate Action.

s: 'Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions' is the title of which SDG?
x: Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions is SDG 16; SDG 12 is Responsible Consumption and Production and SDG 17 is Partnerships for the Goals.

s: Which of the following is NOT one of the 17 Sustainable Development Goals?
x: Blue Economy is linked to SDG 14 but is not an SDG title; Life Below Water is SDG 14.

s: Which of the following is NOT the title of a Sustainable Development Goal?
x: Green Economy is not an SDG; Life on Land is SDG 15, Clean Energy SDG 7 and Partnerships SDG 17.

s: Which of the following is covered under Goal 4, Quality Education?
o: Reduction of remittance costs below 3 percent
Affordable technical, vocational and tertiary education
x: Goal 4 includes affordable technical, vocational and tertiary education, along with equitable schooling, early-childhood care and literacy. The other options relate to Goal 10 or Goal 5.

s: Women's full participation in leadership is a target under which SDG?
o: SDG 16 – Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions
x: SDG 5 (Gender Equality) seeks women's full participation in leadership, besides ending discrimination, violence, child marriage and FGM.

s: Promoting global citizenship and a culture of peace is part of Target 4.7 under which SDG?
o: SDG 16 – Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions
x: Target 4.7 of Goal 4 (Quality Education) seeks that learners promote sustainable development, global citizenship, peace and cultural diversity.

s:
Consider the following statements about SDG 5:
1. It seeks to end child marriage and female genital mutilation.
2. It seeks recognition of unpaid care work.
3. It is the goal on Reduced Inequalities.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: SDG 5 is Gender Equality: it targets child marriage, FGM and unpaid care work. Reduced Inequalities is SDG 10.

s: In which year was the first SDG India Index released?
x: The sequence is Rio+20 2012, Agenda 2030 2015, SDGs in force 2016 and the first SDG India Index 2018.

s: What was India's composite score in the SDG India Index 2023-24?
x: India scored 71 in 2023-24, up from 66 (2020-21) and 57 (2018).

s: Which states topped the SDG India Index 2023-24?
x: Kerala and Uttarakhand topped with 79 each; Bihar was last.

s: As per the SDG India Index 2020-21, what was India's composite score?
x: India scored 66 in the 2020-21 (3rd) edition, up from 57 in 2018; it reached 71 in 2023-24.

s: By how many points did India's overall score improve in the SDG India Index 2020-21?
x: India's overall score rose by 6 points in 2020-21, driven by Goal 6 (Clean Water) and Goal 7 (Clean Energy).

s: Which State was ranked last in the SDG India Index 2023-24?
x: In 2023-24 Kerala and Uttarakhand topped with 79 and Bihar was last.

s: What was India's composite score in the first SDG India Index (2018)?
x: India scored 57 in the first SDG India Index (2018), 66 in 2020-21 and 71 in 2023-24.

s: What was India's composite score in the second edition of the SDG India Index (2019-20)?
x: The second SDG India Index (30 December 2019) showed India's score rising from 57 (2018) to 60.

s: Which State ranked first in the SDG India Index 2019-20?
x: Kerala topped the SDG India Index 2019-20 with 70, followed by Himachal Pradesh with 69.

s: During which session of the UN General Assembly were the Sustainable Development Goals adopted?
x: The UN General Assembly adopted the 2030 Agenda and its 17 SDGs during its 70th session in 2015.

s: Which countries first proposed the idea of the Sustainable Development Goals at Rio+20?
x: Colombia and Guatemala first proposed the SDG idea at the 2012 Rio+20 Conference.

s: Which outcome document of the Rio+20 Conference called for global goals to follow the Millennium Development Goals?
x: The Rio+20 outcome document titled “The Future We Want” called for global goals to follow the MDGs.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the SDGs?
o: Their framework is titled 'Transforming our World: The 2035 Agenda for Sustainable Development'.
They were proposed at Rio+20 in 2012.
x: The framework is titled 'Transforming our World: the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development', not 2035.

s: When did the SDGs of the 2030 Agenda come into force?
x: Adopted at the UNGA 70th session in September 2015, the SDGs came into force on 1 January 2016.

s: What is the motto of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development?
x: 'Leave no one behind' is the motto of the 2030 Agenda.

s: By which documents is Agenda 2030 mainly guided?
o: Geneva Conventions and their Additional Protocols
Vienna Convention and the Montreal Protocol
Universal Declaration of Human Rights and international human-rights treaties
x: Agenda 2030 is guided by the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) together with international human-rights treaties.

s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes the scope of the MDGs from that of the SDGs?
o: MDGs mainly covered developing countries, whereas SDGs are universal.
MDGs were universal, whereas SDGs mainly covered developing countries.
Both MDGs and SDGs mainly covered developed countries.
Both MDGs and SDGs were limited to least-developed countries.
x: The MDGs mainly focused on developing countries, while the SDGs are universal in scope.

s: In the USDG vision, universal access to clean water, sanitation and healthcare is regarded as essential for which of the following?
x: The USDG vision treats universal access to clean water, sanitation and healthcare as essential for human dignity.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the MDGs and SDGs?
o: The MDGs comprised 8 goals and 21 targets
The SDGs comprise 17 goals and 196 targets
x: The SDGs comprise 17 goals and 169 targets, not 196.

s: Under the MDGs, how much did under-5 mortality (per 1,000 live births) decline?
x: Under the MDGs, under-5 mortality fell from 90 to 43 per 1,000 live births, while the maternal mortality ratio fell by 45 percent.

s: The Millennium Development Goals had how many goals and targets?
x: The MDGs (2000-2015) had 8 goals and 21 targets, against the SDGs' 17 goals and 169 targets.

s:
Consider the following statements about the Millennium Development Goals:
1. India achieved the MDG target of halving extreme poverty before 2015.
2. The MDGs applied equally to developed and developing countries.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: India met the target of halving extreme poverty before 2015; the MDGs were mainly for developing countries, unlike the universal SDGs.

s:
Arrange in chronological order:
1. SDGs come into force
2. Rio+20 Conference
3. First SDG India Index
4. Adoption of Agenda 2030
x: Rio+20 (2012) → Agenda 2030 adopted (2015) → SDGs in force (2016) → first SDG India Index (2018).

s: In which year did India's First Five Year Plan begin?
x: The First Five Year Plan began in 1951, the earliest of the development milestones listed with the MDGs (2000) and Agenda 2030 (2015).

s: What were Andhra Pradesh's score and rank in the SDG India Index 2023-24?
x: Andhra Pradesh scored 74 and ranked 9th as a Front Runner; it ranked first only in SDG 7.

s: In the SDG India Index 2023-24, Andhra Pradesh ranked first in which goal?
x: Andhra Pradesh ranks first in SDG 7, though 9th overall.

s: Through which units does the Swarna Andhra KPI Monitoring Framework align with the SDGs?
x: Launched on 13 December 2024, it works through Vision Monitoring Units at state, district and constituency level.

s: When was the Swarna Andhra KPI Monitoring Framework launched?
x: The Swarna Andhra KPI Monitoring Framework was launched on 13 December 2024 and aligns with the SDGs through Vision Monitoring Units.

s: In India, which body coordinates and monitors SDG implementation?
x: NITI Aayog coordinates and monitors the SDGs in India, including the SDG India Index.

s: Which organisation publishes the Sustainable Development Report?
o: United Nations Sustainable Development Solutions Network
x: The Sustainable Development Report is published by the United Nations Sustainable Development Solutions Network (SDSN).

s: Who develops India's SDG National Indicator Framework (NIF)?
x: MoSPI develops the NIF while NITI Aayog coordinates SDG work; the 2026 report tracks 277 indicators.

s: The SDG-NIF Progress Report 2026 tracks how many indicators?
x: The MoSPI SDG-NIF Progress Report 2026 covers 277 indicators across all 17 SDGs; 212 is Andhra Pradesh's indicator count.

s: India's multidimensional poverty fell from 24.85% in 2015-16 to what level in 2019-21?
x: Multidimensional poverty fell from 24.85% (2015-16) to 14.96% (2019-21).

s:
Consider the following statements about the nine themes of Localised SDGs in Gram Panchayats:
1. Women-friendly village is one of the themes.
2. Industrially advanced village is one of the themes.
3. Good governance is one of the themes.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Women-friendly village and good governance are among the nine themes; an industrially advanced village is not a theme.

s: When was the first edition of the North Eastern Region District SDG Index released?
x: The NER District SDG Index (2021-22), a district-level index, was first released in August 2021.

s: Which Ministry promotes the Localised SDGs in Gram Panchayats under nine themes?
o: Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation
x: The Ministry of Panchayati Raj has grouped localised SDGs for Gram Panchayats into nine themes.

s: MGNREGA is associated with which SDG?
x: MGNREGA is linked to SDG 1; NFSA to SDG 2, Ayushman Bharat to SDG 3 and Samagra Shiksha to SDG 4.

s: The Saubhagya scheme is aligned with which SDG?
x: Saubhagya matches SDG 7; Beti Bachao Beti Padhao is SDG 5, Jal Jeevan Mission SDG 6 and Smart Cities SDG 11.

s: Which of the following is associated with SDG 13, Climate Action, in India?
o: National Action Plan on Climate Change and its eight missions
National Food Security Act and POSHAN Abhiyaan
x: India’s National Action Plan on Climate Change, comprising eight missions, is associated with SDG 13.

s: Where was Mission LiFE launched on 20 October 2022?
x: PM Modi launched Mission LiFE with UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres at Kevadia (Ekta Nagar), Gujarat.

s: Mission LiFE aims to mobilise at least how many people for pro-environment behaviour?
x: Mission LiFE aims to mobilise at least one billion 'Pro Planet People' for individual and collective pro-environment behaviour (2022-27).

s: Ayushman Bharat is aligned with which SDG?
x: Ayushman Bharat (PM-JAY, Ayushman Arogya Mandir) maps to SDG 3, Good Health and Well-being.

s: Under Mission LiFE, what are people who adopt pro-environment behaviour called?
x: Mission LiFE aims to make at least one billion people 'Pro Planet People' through individual and collective action.

s: With which SDG are the Smart Cities Mission and AMRUT mainly associated?
x: Smart Cities Mission and AMRUT map to SDG 11, Sustainable Cities and Communities.

s: Beti Bachao Beti Padhao is aligned with which Sustainable Development Goal?
x: Beti Bachao Beti Padhao and gender budgeting serve SDG 5, Gender Equality.

s:
Match the following:
List-I (Scheme)
A. POSHAN Abhiyaan
B. Samagra Shiksha
C. Jal Jeevan Mission
D. PM Ujjwala
List-II (SDG)
1. SDG 7
2. SDG 6
3. SDG 4
4. SDG 2
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
x: POSHAN Abhiyaan = SDG 2; Samagra Shiksha = SDG 4; Jal Jeevan Mission = SDG 6; PM Ujjwala = SDG 7.

s: Along with PM Narendra Modi, who launched Mission LiFE at Kevadia on 20 October 2022?
x: Mission LiFE was launched at Kevadia (Ekta Nagar), Gujarat by PM Modi with UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres.

s: What best-ever rank did India achieve in the Sustainable Development Report 2026?
x: India's best-ever rank is 94th, in SDR 2026. 99th was its 2025 rank, when it first entered the top 100; 109th and 112th are lower ranks from before that.

s: In the Sustainable Development Report 2026, which SDG was identified as India's biggest concern?
x: SDG 2 was India's biggest concern; India lagged on 13 of 17 SDGs and ranked below Bhutan, the Maldives, Nepal and Sri Lanka.

s: In which edition of the Sustainable Development Report did India first enter the top 100?
x: India ranked 99th in SDR 2025, its first time in the top 100; it rose to 94th in SDR 2026.

s: Which country topped the Sustainable Development Report 2025?
x: Finland (87) topped SDR 2025, followed by Sweden and Denmark.

s:
Consider the following statements about India in the Sustainable Development Report 2026:
1. India lags on 13 of the 17 SDGs.
2. India ranks above Bhutan, Nepal and Sri Lanka.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: SDR 2026 ranked India 94th (best ever) but India lags on 13 of 17 SDGs and is still below Bhutan, Maldives, Nepal and Sri Lanka.

s: According to the Sustainable Development Report, about what share of SDG targets are on track globally?
x: The SDR notes that globally only about 17% of SDG targets are on track.

s: The green economy was a central theme of which conference?
x: The green economy, which decouples growth from resource use and pollution, was a central theme of Rio+20 (2012).

s: Green jobs are work that does which of the following?
o: Is done only in the forestry sector
x: Green jobs are work in farming, industry, services or administration that preserves or restores environmental quality.

s: Which of the following statements about green technology is NOT correct?
o: It pollutes less than conventional technology
It uses resources in a sustainable way
It recycles more of its waste
It is not expensive for developing countries
x: High cost is the main barrier to green technology in developing countries, so the last statement is wrong.

s: What does a green economy seek to do?
o: Decouple economic growth from resource use and pollution
Increase the use of natural resources
x: A green economy reduces environmental risks by decoupling growth from resource use and pollution; it was the central theme of Rio+20.

s: In response to what was the Partnership for Action on Green Economy (PAGE) launched in 2013?
x: PAGE was launched in 2013 in response to the call made at Rio+20 for action towards greener and more inclusive economies.

s: In which year was the UNEP Green Economy Initiative launched?
x: UNEP's Green Economy Initiative began in 2008; Rio+20 was 2012 and PAGE 2013.

s: Which Ministry launched the Green Skill Development Programme in 2017?
o: Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
Ministry of New and Renewable Energy
Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship alone
x: The Green Skill Development Programme was launched in 2017 by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change.

s: The Green Skill Development Programme builds on which network?
x: The MoEFCC launched the GSDP in 2017 on the ENVIS network.

s: Which of the following is NOT a sector the Green Skill Development Programme trains youth for?
x: GSDP trains youth in biodiversity conservation, pollution monitoring, waste management, forestry and wildlife; semiconductor manufacturing is not one.

s: Who introduced the 12 Principles of Green Chemistry (1998)?
x: Paul Anastas and John Warner introduced the 12 Principles of Green Chemistry in 1998.

s: Green chemistry and cleaner production serve the goals of EIA and LCA because they:
o: Deal only with final waste disposal
Reduce waste and pollution across the product life cycle
Increase output regardless of resource use
x: Green chemistry and cleaner production minimise waste and pollution throughout the product life cycle, supporting the objectives of EIA and LCA.

s: What is the core idea of the 12 Principles of Green Chemistry?
x: The 12 Principles (1998, Anastas and Warner) rest on preventing waste rather than cleaning it up.

s: What is green chemistry applied to the design, use and disposal of medicines called?
x: Green Pharmacy is green chemistry applied to medicines.

s: Which of the following is among the priority waste streams for which circular-economy action plans were drawn up in India?
x: NITI Aayog and MoEFCC committees drew up plans for streams including plastics, e-waste, batteries, tyres and metals.

s: What does a circular economy mainly promote?
o: A take-make-dispose pattern of resource use
Use of fossil fuels alone for energy
Reuse, recycling and repair of materials to reduce waste
Growth through more extraction of raw materials
x: A circular economy keeps materials in use through reuse, recycling and repair, so waste becomes a resource.

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. In a linear economy, waste is the end point.
2. In a circular economy, waste is treated as a resource.
3. The circular economy focuses only on carbon and fossil fuels.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: The linear model ends in waste while the circular model reuses it; the circular economy is not only about carbon.

s: What is the European Green Deal's legislative package to cut greenhouse gases by at least 55% by 2030 (vs 1990) called?
x: The package is 'Fit for 55'; the Deal was launched in December 2019 and targets climate neutrality by 2050.

s: Which of the following pairs relating to the European Green Deal is INCORRECTLY matched?
o: Biodiversity Strategy – Support for affected regions
Farm to Fork – Sustainable food system
Circular Economy Action Plan – Resource efficiency and recycling
Just Transition Fund – Support for affected regions
x: The Biodiversity Strategy protects and restores ecosystems; support for affected regions is the Just Transition Fund.

s: What does the Just Transition Fund under the European Green Deal provide?
x: The Just Transition Fund supports affected regions; ecosystem protection is the Biodiversity Strategy.

s: By which year does the European Green Deal aim to make the EU climate-neutral?
x: The European Green Deal (2019) targets a climate-neutral EU by 2050 and a 55% cut by 2030.

s: Why is a clear taxonomy considered necessary in relation to greenwashing?
o: To replace life-cycle assessment with a single carbon figure
To help regulators curb greenwashing and transition washing
To remove all environmental regulations from financial markets
To classify only species threatened with extinction
x: A clear taxonomy helps regulators identify and curb greenwashing as well as transition washing.

s: What is meant by 'greenwashing'?
o: False or exaggerated claims that a product or firm is environment-friendly
x: Greenwashing means making false or exaggerated green claims about a product, firm or investment.

s: What does the RBI Green Deposit Framework mainly enable banks to do?
o: Raise deposits earmarked for green lending
Set the national climate finance taxonomy
Finance social projects without accepting deposits
x: The RBI Green Deposit Framework allows banks to raise deposits specifically earmarked for green lending. It has been in force since 2023.

s: Which institution pioneered green bonds in 2007?
x: The EIB pioneered green bonds in 2007, followed by the World Bank in 2008; proceeds fund environment-friendly projects.

s: How much did India's first Sovereign Green Bond issue in 2023 amount to?
x: Sovereign Green Bonds were announced in Budget 2022-23, the framework came in 2022 and the first issue in 2023 was Rs 8,000 crore.

s: Which country issued the world's first sovereign blue bond in 2018?
x: Seychelles issued the first sovereign blue bond in 2018.

s:
Consider the following statements about green taxonomy in India:
1. India has already established a final green taxonomy for all sectors.
2. The Climate Finance Taxonomy was announced in Budget 2024-25.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Only 2 is correct: the Climate Finance Taxonomy was announced in Budget 2024-25, but a final all-sector green taxonomy is still a key gap.

s: Which body has planned India's first blue bond?
x: Sagarmala Finance Corporation plans India's first blue bond, Rs 1,000 crore, in FY 2026-27.

s: India's Sovereign Green Bonds were announced in which Union Budget?
x: Sovereign Green Bonds were announced in Budget 2022-23; the first issue (Rs 8,000 crore) came in 2023.

s: Which Ministry has brought out a Green Steel Taxonomy?
x: The Ministry of Steel has a Green Steel Taxonomy; the climate finance taxonomy is from the Ministry of Finance.

s: For what are the proceeds of a blue bond used?
x: Blue bonds fund ocean and water projects; Seychelles issued the world's first sovereign blue bond in 2018.

s: What is MSE-GIFT?
o: A green finance scheme for MSMEs
A GST relief for small exporters
x: MSE-GIFT provides green finance for MSMEs (2023-26).

s: According to the International Capital Market Association (ICMA), what is a sustainability bond?
o: A bond whose proceeds finance a combination of both green and social projects
A bond whose proceeds finance only renewable energy projects
A bond issued only by sovereign governments
A bond linked to the issuer's ESG rating
x: ICMA's Sustainability Bond Guidelines define sustainability bonds as bonds whose proceeds finance or refinance a combination of green and social projects.

s: For what are the proceeds of a social bond used?
o: New and existing projects with positive social outcomes
x: ICMA's Social Bond Principles define social bonds as use-of-proceeds bonds for projects with positive social outcomes.

s: In India, who sets Business Responsibility and Sustainability Reporting (BRSR)?
x: BRSR is set by SEBI, which also regulates ESG Rating Providers; the top 1,000 listed companies publish audited ESG metrics yearly.

s: From which companies does BRSR require audited ESG metrics every year?
x: SEBI's BRSR applies to the top 1,000 listed companies, which publish audited ESG metrics every year.

s: In India, who regulates ESG Rating Providers?
x: SEBI regulates ESG Rating Providers, as it sets the BRSR.

s: What are the three pillars of ESG?
x: ESG stands for Environmental, Social and Governance.

s: In which year did MoEFCC notify the Green Credit Programme?
x: MoEFCC notified the Green Credit Programme in October 2023.

s: What is the annual production target of India's Green Hydrogen Mission (outlay Rs 19,744 crore)?
x: The Mission targets 5 MMT a year and is linked with the net-zero goal for 2070.

s: Who prepared the Draft National Resource Efficiency Policy, 2019?
x: The draft policy was prepared by MoEFCC; the Ministry of Steel issued the Green Steel Taxonomy.

s: Which items do India's Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) regimes cover?
o: Plastic packaging, e-waste, batteries and tyres
x: The EPR regimes cover plastic packaging, e-waste, batteries and tyres.

s: What kind of instrument is the Green Credit Programme notified by MoEFCC in October 2023?
o: A market-based incentive for voluntary environmental actions
x: The Green Credit Programme is a market-based incentive for voluntary actions such as tree plantation and water conservation.

s: Which new body does the Draft National Resource Efficiency Policy, 2019 propose?
x: The draft NREP 2019 (MoEFCC) promotes secondary raw materials and a National Resource Efficiency Authority.

s: Under AMRUT 2.0, treated used water is to meet what share of city demand and industrial demand respectively?
x: AMRUT 2.0 targets reuse of treated water for 20% of city demand and 40% of industrial demand.

s: India's Green Hydrogen Mission is linked to India's net zero target of which year?
x: The Green Hydrogen Mission (Rs 19,744 crore, 5 MMT a year) supports India's net zero by 2070.

s:
Consider the following statements about chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs):
1. They contribute to global warming.
2. They contribute to ozone depletion.
3. They have been used in refrigerators, air-conditioners and aerosol propellants.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: All three are correct: CFCs are greenhouse gases and ozone depleters, and they were used in refrigerators, ACs and aerosols.

s:
Consider the following statements about ozone destruction:
1. Chlorine and bromine atoms can catalytically destroy stratospheric ozone molecules.
2. Each chlorine or bromine atom is consumed permanently in its first reaction.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Only 1 is correct: the atoms act catalytically and are not consumed in the first reaction.

s: Halons are roughly how many times more potent ozone depleters than CFCs?
x: Halons, which contain bromine, are about 100 times more potent than CFCs.

s: When did the Montreal Protocol enter into force?
x: Adopted on 16 September 1987, it entered into force on 1 January 1989; 1991 is when the Multilateral Fund was set up.

s: What does the Multilateral Fund under the Montreal Protocol mainly provide?
o: Technical and financial assistance to developing countries
Loans to CFC manufacturers in developed countries
Compensation to developed countries for HFC phase-down
Funds for climate adaptation in small island states
x: The Multilateral Fund gives developing countries technical and financial assistance to implement their ODS phase-out obligations.

s: In which year was the Vienna Convention, the framework treaty for protection of the ozone layer, adopted?
x: The Vienna Convention was adopted in 1985; the Montreal Protocol, its action treaty, followed in 1987.

s:
Consider the following statements about the ozone treaty system:
1. The Multilateral Fund (1991) provides aid to developing countries.
2. The Kigali Amendment (2016) provides for the phase-down of HFCs.
3. The Multilateral Fund was created for the phase-down of HFCs.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: The Multilateral Fund (1991) aids developing countries; the phase-down of HFCs is the work of the Kigali Amendment, so 3 is wrong.

s: Which was the first UN treaty to achieve universal ratification?
x: With 198 Parties, the Montreal Protocol (with the Vienna Convention) is the first universally ratified UN treaty.

s: How many Parties does the Montreal Protocol have?
x: The Montreal Protocol has 198 Parties - universal ratification.

s: Where is the Ozone Secretariat of the Montreal Protocol located?
x: The Ozone Secretariat sits in Nairobi.

s: Where was the Montreal Protocol signed in 1987?
x: It was signed on 16 September 1987 at Montreal, Canada - not Helsinki.

s: About how much of ozone-depleting substances had been phased out under the Montreal Protocol by 2024?
x: About 99% of ODS had been phased out by 2024; the protocol avoids 0.5-1 degree C of warming by 2050.

s: What was the Thirty-Seventh Meeting of the Parties (MOP37) to the Montreal Protocol mainly focused on?
o: Elimination of all persistent organic pollutants
x: MOP37 focused on implementation of the Kigali Amendment.

s: What does the Cartagena Protocol deal with?
x: Cartagena covers biosafety and LMOs; Montreal covers ODS, Nagoya access and benefit sharing and Kigali the phase-down of HFCs.

s: Which of the following pairs is wrongly matched?
o: Nagoya Protocol (2010) – Access and benefit sharing
x: The Cartagena Protocol on biosafety was adopted in 2000, not 2010. The Nagoya Protocol was adopted in 2010 and the Kigali Amendment in 2016.

s: Which treaty introduced binding emission targets for developed countries?
x: The Kyoto Protocol set binding targets for developed countries; the UNFCCC is the framework and Paris set the 1.5°C goal.

s: Which international treaty deals with hazardous waste?
x: Hazardous waste comes under the Basel Convention; ozone is under the Vienna Convention, ODS phase-out under Montreal and the human environment under the Stockholm Declaration.

s: Ozone is concentrated predominantly in which layer of the atmosphere, and at about what altitude?
x: Ozone is concentrated mainly in the stratosphere, approximately between 10 and 50 km above Earth. This layer absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation.

s: Below what level of total column ozone is an ozone hole conventionally identified?
x: The term ozone hole is used when total ozone falls below 220 Dobson Units.

s: What does 1 Dobson Unit (DU) represent?
o: 0.1 mm of pure ozone at 0°C and 1 atm
0.01 mm of pure ozone at 0°C and 1 atm
0.01 mm of pure ozone at 25°C and 1 atm
1 mm of pure ozone at 0°C and 1 atm
x: One Dobson Unit is a layer of pure ozone 0.01 mm thick at 0°C and 1 atmosphere. The traps change the thickness or the temperature.

s: In the ozone-oxygen cycle, by the action of what is ozone formed?
x: UV radiation splits O2 and forms O3 - the ozone-oxygen cycle.

s: When is the seasonal thinning of the ozone layer over Antarctica most pronounced?
o: Southern Hemisphere autumn, March to May
Southern Hemisphere summer, December to February
Southern Hemisphere spring, approximately August to November
Northern Hemisphere spring, March to May
x: The Antarctic ozone hole is a seasonal phenomenon, with maximum thinning during Southern Hemisphere spring, approximately August to November.

s: How do polar stratospheric clouds contribute to ozone destruction?
o: Absorb all incoming solar radiation before it reaches the stratosphere
Convert oxygen directly into carbon dioxide
Prevent the return of sunlight to the polar vortex
Convert stable chlorine compounds into active forms on their surfaces in extreme cold
x: In the extremely cold polar vortex, polar stratospheric clouds provide surfaces that convert stable chlorine into active forms. When sunlight returns, these forms catalytically destroy ozone.

s: By about which year is the ozone layer over the Antarctic projected to recover?
x: Recovery is projected by 2040 for most of the world, 2045 over the Arctic and 2066 over the Antarctic.

s: Who first reported the ozone hole over Antarctica in 1985?
o: Members of the Indian Antarctic Expedition
Scientists of the Soviet Antarctic Expedition
Scientists of the British Antarctic Survey
x: The Antarctic ozone hole was first reported in 1985 by British Antarctic Survey scientists.

s: By about which year is the ozone layer over most of the world projected to return to 1980 levels?
x: Recovery to 1980 levels is projected by 2040 for most of the world, 2045 for the Arctic and 2066 for the Antarctic.

s: By about which year is the ozone layer over the Arctic projected to return to 1980 levels?
x: Projected recovery: most of the world 2040, Arctic 2045, Antarctic 2066.

s: Why are HFCs, which replaced ozone-depleting substances in air-conditioners and refrigerators, a concern?
o: Have very high global warming potential
Release chlorine atoms in the stratosphere
x: HFCs do not deplete ozone but have very high global warming potential.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about ozone-depleting substances?
o: HFCs are ozone-depleting substances and the main cause of the ozone hole
Methyl bromide is used as an agricultural fumigant and in quarantine treatment
Carbon tetrachloride and methyl chloroform are associated with solvent use
Halons contain bromine and are used in portable fire extinguishers
x: HFCs are non-ODS substitutes with high global warming potential; CFCs are the main cause of ozone depletion.

s: Which refrigerant is used in large cold-storage plants?
x: Liquid ammonia cools large cold stores; Freon was used in home refrigerators, SO₂ was an early refrigerant and N₂O is laughing gas.

s:
Consider the following statements about ozone-depleting substances and their uses:
1. Halons are used in portable fire extinguishers.
2. HCFCs are mainly used in portable fire extinguishers.
3. Methyl bromide is used as an agricultural fumigant.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Halons serve portable fire extinguishers and methyl bromide is a fumigant; HCFCs are transitional CFC substitutes, not extinguisher agents.

s: Which chemicals react in a soda-acid fire extinguisher to produce carbon dioxide?
o: Sodium bicarbonate and dilute sulphuric acid
x: In a soda-acid extinguisher, NaHCO3 reacts with dilute H2SO4 to give CO2.

s: For what is methyl bromide, an ozone-depleting substance, mainly used?
x: Methyl bromide is an agricultural fumigant; halons are used in fire extinguishers.

s: What does World Ozone Day on 16 September mark?
o: Discovery of the Antarctic ozone hole
x: 16 September marks the signing of the Montreal Protocol in 1987.

s: What is the theme of World Ozone Day 2026?
o: Global Action for a Cooler Planet
Montreal Protocol: Fixing the Ozone Layer
x: The 2026 theme, 'Global Action for a Cooler Planet', marks 10 years of the Kigali Amendment.

s: In which year did the UN General Assembly declare 16 September as World Ozone Day?
x: UNGA declared it on 19 December 1994.

s: Which gases does the Kigali Amendment (2016) to the Montreal Protocol phase down?
x: Kigali phases down HFCs, which do not deplete ozone but have very high global warming potential; it entered into force on 1 January 2019.

s: In which year did India ratify the Kigali Amendment to the Montreal Protocol?
x: India ratified the Kigali Amendment in 2021. 2016 is the year it was adopted at Kigali, 2019 the year it entered into force, and 2028 is India's HFC freeze year.

s: In which year does India (Group 2) freeze HFCs under the Kigali Amendment?
x: India's baseline years are 2024-26 and its freeze year is 2028; its final cut is 85% by 2047.

s: After which date has MoEFCC directed that no environmental clearance be granted for new or additional HFC production?
x: MoEFCC directed Central and State authorities to stop granting environmental clearances for new or additional HFC production after 31 December 2027.

s: By which year must India cut HFCs by 85% under the Kigali Amendment?
x: India (Group 2) has a 2024-26 baseline, a 2028 freeze and an 85% cut by 2047.

s: When did the Kigali Amendment come into force?
x: Adopted in 2016 at Kigali, Rwanda, it came into force on 1 January 2019.

s: In which city was the Kigali Amendment to the Montreal Protocol adopted in 2016?
x: The Kigali Amendment was adopted in 2016 at Kigali, Rwanda; it came into force on 1 January 2019.

s: What is India's baseline period for the HFC phase-down under the Kigali Amendment?
x: India (Group 2) has baseline 2024-26, freeze 2028 and an 85% cut by 2047.

s: Along with India, which of the following countries is in Group 2 under the Kigali Amendment?
x: Group 2 includes India, the Gulf states, Iran, Iraq and Pakistan; China is in Group 1.

s: The Kigali Amendment is expected to avoid up to how much global warming by 2100?
x: Cutting HFC use by 80-85% by the late 2040s can avoid up to 0.5 degree C of warming by 2100.

s: Under which Act were the Ozone-Depleting Substances (Regulation and Control) Rules, 2000 framed?
o: Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act
x: The ODS (Regulation and Control) Rules, 2000 were framed under the Environment (Protection) Act.

s: Which is India's National Ozone Unit?
o: Ozone Cell in the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
x: India’s Ozone Cell in the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change functions as the National Ozone Unit.

s: Up to which year does the time horizon of the India Cooling Action Plan extend?
x: ICAP has a 20-year horizon extending to 2037-38.

s: Which one of the following is NOT one of the six thematic areas of the India Cooling Action Plan?
x: The six thematic areas are space cooling in buildings, cold chain, servicing sector, domestic or indigenous production, research and development, and transport. Coal-based power generation is not one of them.

s: By how much does the India Cooling Action Plan (2019) aim to reduce cooling demand and refrigerant demand, respectively, by 2037-38?
x: ICAP targets a 20-25% cut in cooling demand and a 25-30% cut in refrigerant demand by 2037-38, plus training 1 lakh servicing technicians. Option B swaps the two figures, and options C and D give ranges not in the plan.

s: By which year was methyl bromide to be phased out in India?
x: Halons were phased out by 2001, CFCs in manufacturing by 2003, CTC, methyl chloroform and CFCs in MDIs by 2010 and methyl bromide by 2015.

s: Under India's ODS phase-out schedule, up to when were HCFCs permitted?
x: HCFCs were allowed under the stated Indian schedule up to 1 January 2040.

s: India was the first developing country to fully phase out which substance in rigid foam?
x: Under HPMP Stage-II, India fully phased out HCFC-141b in rigid foam.

s: By which date were halons (except essential uses) phased out in India?
x: India phased out halons by 1 Jan 2001, CFCs in manufacturing by 2003, CTC by 2010 and methyl bromide by 2015.

s: When did the Ban Amendment to the Basel Convention, banning hazardous-waste exports from OECD/EU countries and Liechtenstein to other countries, come into force?
x: The Ban Amendment came into force on 5 December 2019 to stop rich countries dumping hazardous waste on poorer ones.

s: The Prior Informed Consent mechanism for implementing the Basel Convention in India operates under which rules?
o: Hazardous and Other Wastes (Management and Transboundary Movement) Rules, 2016
x: India implements the Basel Convention through the Prior Informed Consent mechanism under the Hazardous and Other Wastes (Management and Transboundary Movement) Rules, 2016.

s: In which year did India accede to the Rotterdam Convention?
x: The Rotterdam Convention entered into force in 2004 and India acceded in 2005.

s: In India, the Basel, Rotterdam and Stockholm conventions are coordinated by which unit of MoEFCC?
x: The BRS conventions are coordinated by the Hazardous Substances Management Division; the Ozone Cell is the National Ozone Unit for the Montreal Protocol.

s: What is chlorpyrifos, added to Stockholm Convention Annex A in 2025?
x: Chlorpyrifos is a neurotoxic insecticide; long-chain PFCAs are PFAS 'forever chemicals' and medium-chain chlorinated paraffins are used in plastics.

s: What does the Prior Informed Consent (PIC) procedure under the Rotterdam Convention imply?
o: An importing country must agree before a listed chemical is exported to it
Only the exporting country can prohibit the use of a chemical
Chemicals may be exported only after approval by the World Health Organization
An exporting country may export any chemical without notification
x: Under the PIC procedure, the importing country must provide consent before a listed hazardous chemical can be exported to it.

s: Which one of the following is NOT included among the initial ‘dirty dozen’ POPs?
x: DDT, PCBs, dioxins and furans were among the initial 12 POPs. Chlorpyrifos was added to Annex A in 2025, not included in the initial dirty dozen.

s: In which year did India ratify the Stockholm Convention on POPs?
x: The Convention was adopted in 2001 and entered into force in 2004; India ratified it in 2006 and ratified seven additional POPs in 2020.

s: The Minamata Convention mainly seeks protection from which of the following?
o: Emission of HFCs from cooling appliances
Man-made emissions of mercury and mercury compounds
x: The Minamata Convention protects human health and the environment from anthropogenic emissions of mercury and mercury compounds across the mercury lifecycle.

s: Which body assesses candidate chemicals for possible listing as Persistent Organic Pollutants under the Stockholm Convention?
x: The POPs Review Committee, or POPRC, assesses candidate chemicals for possible listing.

s: Which of the following is NOT identified as a major source of mercury emissions?
o: Solar photovoltaic panels in normal operation
x: Major sources include coal-fired power plants, artisanal and small-scale gold mining, industrial processes and waste. Solar photovoltaic panels in normal operation are not listed as a major source.

s: With what is the name 'Minamata' associated?
o: A major oil spill in the Pacific Ocean
A mercury-poisoning episode caused by contaminated factory wastewater in Japan
x: The Convention is named after Minamata, Japan, where factory wastewater contaminated local fish with mercury and poisoned people in the 1950s. The illness became known as Minamata disease.

s: Which of the following pairs is wrongly matched?
x: Mercury comes under the Minamata Convention. The Rotterdam Convention deals with prior informed consent for hazardous chemicals and pesticides.

s:
Consider the following statements about the Annexes of the Stockholm Convention:
1. DDT is in Annex B, with limited use allowed for malaria control.
2. Aldrin is in Annex A.
3. Dioxins and furans are in Annex B.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: DDT is in Annex B (restriction) and aldrin in Annex A (elimination); dioxins and furans are in Annex C (unintentional by-products).

s: Persistent Organic Pollutants are characterised by which combination of properties?
o: Toxicity, long persistence, bioaccumulation and long-distance transport
Radioactivity, water solubility and immediate evaporation
High biodegradability, low toxicity and limited mobility
Short persistence, rapid breakdown and local movement only
x: POPs are toxic chemicals that persist for long periods, build up in living tissue and travel long distances.

s: By what name are long-chain PFCAs, added to Stockholm Convention Annex A in 2025, known?
x: Long-chain PFCAs are PFAS 'forever chemicals' found in cookware, added to Annex A in 2025.

s: In 2020, India ratified how many more POPs under the Stockholm Convention?
x: India ratified 7 more POPs in 2020, including chlordecone and hexabromobiphenyl.

s: How many chemicals are now listed under the Stockholm Convention?
x: From the initial 'dirty dozen', the list has grown to 37 (34 by 2023 plus 3 in 2025).

s: Along with the Ministry of Agriculture, which Ministry is India's Designated National Authority for the Rotterdam Convention?
x: The DNAs are the Ministry of Chemicals & Fertilisers and the Ministry of Agriculture.

s: By which year is dental amalgam to be phased out under the Minamata Convention?
x: The Minamata Convention phases out dental amalgam by 2034.

s: Which convention deals with mercury?
x: Minamata concerns mercury; Basel concerns waste, Rotterdam prior consent in trade and Stockholm persistent chemicals.

s: In which year was the Minamata Convention on mercury adopted?
x: The Minamata Convention was adopted in 2013 and entered into force in 2017.

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Stockholm Convention on POPs was adopted in 2001 and came into force in 2004.
2. The Rotterdam Convention came into force in 2004.
3. The Minamata Convention came into force in 2013.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Stockholm (2001, in force 2004) and Rotterdam (in force 2004) are right; Minamata was adopted in 2013 and came into force in 2017.

s: In which year did the Minamata Convention on mercury come into force?
x: The Minamata Convention was adopted in 2013 and came into force in 2017.

s: Under which Annex of the Stockholm Convention are dioxins and furans, produced as unintentional by-products, listed?
x: Annex A = elimination (aldrin), Annex B = restriction (DDT), Annex C = unintentional by-products (dioxins, furans).

s: Which of the following conventions share one joint secretariat under UNEP?
x: The Basel, Rotterdam and Stockholm (BRS) conventions share one joint secretariat under UNEP.

s: What does Annex III of the Rotterdam Convention list?
o: Pesticides and industrial chemicals banned or severely restricted by Parties
Persistent organic pollutants to be eliminated
x: Annex III lists pesticides and industrial chemicals banned or severely restricted, which are subject to the PIC procedure.

s:
Arrange the following treaties in chronological order of adoption:
A. Kyoto Protocol
B. Basel Convention
C. Cartagena Protocol
D. Vienna Convention
x: The Vienna Convention was adopted in 1985, the Basel Convention in 1989, the Kyoto Protocol in 1997 and the Cartagena Protocol in 2000.

s:
Assertion (A): Ozone depletion increases the incidence of skin cancer.
Reason (R): Ozone depletion increases exposure to UV-B radiation, which can cause skin cancer and DNA damage.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
x: Both are true and R explains A: more UV-B reaches the surface, causing DNA damage, skin cancer, cataracts and immune suppression.

s: Which of the following can increased UV-B exposure cause in humans?
o: Night blindness from vitamin A deficiency
x: UV-B causes skin cancer, cataracts, immune suppression and DNA damage.

s: By about how much does a 1% loss of ozone raise harmful UV radiation?
x: A 1% ozone loss raises harmful UV by about 2%.

s: Which of the following is NOT an effect of increased UV-B radiation?
o: Reduced photosynthesis in rice and wheat
Damage to phytoplankton and fish larvae
x: UV-B damages plankton and disrupts the food chain; it does not boost phytoplankton growth.

s: According to the Rivet Popper Hypothesis, the loss of which kind of species may destabilise or collapse an ecosystem?
x: The hypothesis holds that losing a few species may seem harmless, but losing key or keystone species may collapse an ecosystem.

s: Timber, fibre, medicines and genetic material sold commercially are examples of which value of biodiversity?
x: Commercially sold goods are productive use value; fuelwood, fodder and wild food used locally without sale are consumptive use value.

s: What is the possible future use of an undiscovered medicinal compound or a new crop gene called?
x: Option value refers to possible future benefits, including undiscovered medicines and useful crop genes.

s: For whom was the Dasgupta Review (2021), which treats nature as an asset, prepared?
x: Partha Dasgupta prepared the Review for the UK Treasury; it argues that GDP ignores nature's depreciation.

s: TEEB, hosted by UNEP, began in 2007 as an initiative of which group?
x: TEEB began from a G8+5 initiative in 2007 and is hosted by UNEP, not the World Economic Forum.

s: What is the role of biodiversity in sustainable development?
o: It mainly increases the area available for urban expansion
It supports ecosystem services such as food, water and air quality
It replaces the need for conservation laws
It matters only for its aesthetic and recreational value
x: Biodiversity underpins sustainable development by supporting ecosystem services such as food, water and air quality. It does not provide land for urban expansion, does not replace conservation laws, and its value is not limited to aesthetics and recreation.

s: Fuelwood, fodder and wild food used locally and not sold are examples of which value of biodiversity?
x: Consumptive value is local use without sale; productive value is commercial sale.

s: Which of the following pairs (value of biodiversity – example) is correctly matched?
x: Aesthetic value covers beauty and ecotourism; fuelwood is consumptive, sacred groves social and sold timber productive.

s: Who proposed the Rivet popper hypothesis?
x: Paul Ehrlich compared an ecosystem to an aeroplane and species to its rivets.

s: Who led TEEB (The Economics of Ecosystems and Biodiversity)?
x: TEEB, a G8+5 initiative of 2007 hosted by UNEP, was led by Pavan Sukhdev.

s: From which plant does the caterpillar of the Monarch butterfly get the cardenolides that make the butterfly toxic?
x: Monarch caterpillars eat milkweed, whose cardenolides make the adult butterfly toxic to predators.

s: What does species diversity, the variety of species in an area, take into account?
o: Only the number of species, irrespective of abundance
Only variation in genes within a single species
Only the variety of climatic zones
x: Species diversity is the variety of species in an area and includes both richness and abundance.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about ecosystem diversity?
o: It refers to the variety of ecosystems in an area
Boreal conifers cannot do the job of tropical deciduous trees in every context
Rainforests, deciduous forests and boreal ecosystems are examples of different ecosystems
One ecosystem can always replace the functions of another
x: One ecosystem cannot simply replace another's functions.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct?
o: Endemic species are restricted to a particular geographical area.
Invasive alien species harm native ecosystems or species.
Alien species are introduced outside their natural range.
Genetic diversity refers to the variety of ecosystems.
x: Genetic diversity is variation within a species; the variety of ecosystems is ecosystem diversity.

s: Who coined the word 'biodiversity'?
x: Walter G. Rosen coined the word (1985) and E.O. Wilson popularised it; alpha, beta and gamma diversity terms come from Whittaker.

s: The CBD defines biodiversity as variability among living organisms from terrestrial, marine and other aquatic ecosystems and the ____ of which they are part.
x: The CBD definition covers organisms from all these sources together with the ecological complexes to which they belong.

s: What do species richness and species evenness refer to, respectively?
o: Relative abundance and total number of species
Total number of species and their relative abundance
Change between ecosystems and total regional diversity
x: Species richness is the number of species, while species evenness indicates their relative abundance. Low evenness means that a few species dominate.

s: What is the total diversity across the ecosystems of a whole region called?
x: Gamma diversity is the regional total; beta diversity is species turnover between ecosystems and alpha is diversity within one area.

s: Which pair of indices is used for measuring species diversity?
o: Simpson index and Human Development Index
x: The Shannon-Wiener and Simpson indices are measures of species diversity.

s: Forest A has 2 tigers, 6 deer and 7 rabbits; Forest B has 1 tiger, 6 deer and 8 rabbits. Compared with Forest B, what does Forest A have?
x: Both have three species and 15 individuals, but individuals are more equally distributed in Forest A, so it is more even.

s: What is functional diversity mainly concerned with?
o: the number of crop species cultivated by humans
the range of ecological roles performed by organisms
only the number of fossil species in a region
the geographical extent of a biosphere reserve
x: Functional diversity measures the range of ecological roles. Its components include functional richness, functional evenness and functional divergence.

s: Who introduced the terms alpha, beta and gamma diversity?
x: R.H. Whittaker introduced the terms alpha, beta and gamma diversity.

s: Which diversity measures the turnover of species between ecosystems along a gradient?
x: Beta diversity is diversity between ecosystems (species turnover); alpha is within a habitat and gamma is regional.

s: Which of the following is a recognised explanation for the greater biodiversity of tropical regions?
o: Long, undisturbed evolutionary history without glaciation
x: Tropical richness is linked to long evolutionary time without glaciation, a stable climate and more solar energy and productivity.

s: About how many living species have been described so far?
x: About 1.5 million species have been described; E.O. Wilson estimated 10-50 million species in all, including undescribed ones.

s: A survey of ants found about how many species at the equator, against about 10 near the North Pole?
x: The survey found about 10 ant species near the North Pole and up to about 2,000 at the equator, showing the latitudinal gradient.

s: Which of the following correctly identifies the ecosystems with the greatest species richness on land and in the sea, respectively?
x: Tropical rainforests or tropical moist forests are the richest terrestrial ecosystems, while coral reefs are the richest marine ecosystems.

s: Which is the richest group among recorded animal species?
x: Over 70% of recorded species are animals and insects are the richest animal group; plants account for about 22%.

s: With whom is the estimate of 10–50 million total species on Earth associated?
x: Wilson (1992) estimated 10–50 million species; Robert May estimated about 7 million.

s: At about how many did Robert May estimate the total number of species on Earth?
x: May estimated about 7 million; 1.5 million is the number described so far.

s: Plants make up about what share of recorded species?
x: Plants are about 22% of recorded species; animals are over 70%.

s:
Assertion (A): Most butterfly species are found in the tropics.
Reason (R): Butterflies cannot tolerate low temperatures.
o: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
x: Both are true and R explains A: butterflies cannot bear the cold, so most species live in the warm tropics.

s: Who proposed the species-area relationship (log S = log C + Z log A)?
x: Humboldt proposed the species-area relationship; Paul Ehrlich proposed the rivet popper hypothesis.

s: Who classified India into biogeographic zones and provinces in the standard scheme associated with the year 1988?
o: Rodgers and Panwar under the Wildlife Institute of India
Alexander von Humboldt under the Zoological Survey of India
Rodgers and Panwar under the Botanical Survey of India
Madhav Gadgil and Panwar under the Indian Council of Forestry Research
x: The classification was prepared by Rodgers and Panwar under the Wildlife Institute of India in 1988.

s: Andhra Pradesh falls under which biogeographic zone?
x: Andhra Pradesh is included in the Deccan biogeographic zone.

s: Which two biogeographical realms are represented in India?
x: India covers the Palearctic and Indo-Malayan biogeographical realms.

s: Which one of the following is the largest biogeographic zone of India?
x: The Deccan Peninsula is the largest biogeographic zone of India and covers about 42% of the country's land area.

s: Which of the following is a province of the Deccan Peninsula biogeographic zone?
x: The Deccan Peninsula provinces are Central Highlands, Chotanagpur, Eastern Highlands, Central Plateau and Deccan South.

s: The Trans-Himalaya biogeographic zone covers about what share of India's land?
x: The Trans-Himalaya covers only about 5.7%; about 42% is the share of the Deccan Peninsula, the largest zone.

s: Under the Rodgers and Panwar scheme, India's biogeographic zones fall into how many biomes?
x: There are 2 realms, 5 biomes, 10 zones and 25 provinces.

s: Which biogeographic zone of India records the highest number of faunal species?
x: The Himalaya has the most faunal species (30,377); the Deccan Peninsula is the largest zone.

s: How many provinces does the Deccan Peninsula biogeographic zone have?
x: The Deccan Peninsula has 5 provinces, including Central Highlands, Chotanagpur and Deccan South.

s: Into how many biogeographic zones is India divided under the Rodgers and Panwar scheme?
x: Rodgers and Panwar (WII, 1988) gave 2 realms, 5 biomes, 10 zones and 25 provinces.

s: Which is India's only ape?
x: The hoolock gibbon of North-East India is India's only ape.

s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
x: The Nilgiri tahr is restricted to the Western Ghats, not the Eastern Ghats. The hoolock gibbon occurs in the North-East, the Asiatic lion in Gir and the lion-tailed macaque in the Western Ghats.

s: Which one of the following species is naturally found only in India among the listed fauna?
x: The Asiatic lion is naturally restricted to India, particularly the Gir region of Gujarat. The other listed species also occur outside India or have wider natural ranges.

s: Which of the following pairs (species – natural range) is INCORRECTLY matched?
o: Hoolock gibbon – Bhitarkanika, Sundarbans and Andaman and Nicobar
Saltwater crocodile – Bhitarkanika, Sundarbans and Andaman and Nicobar
x: The hoolock gibbon occurs in North-East India south of the Brahmaputra; Bhitarkanika and the Sundarbans are saltwater-crocodile habitats.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
x: The Nilgiri tahr lives in Eravikulam (Kerala). The Asiatic lion is in Gir, the one-horned rhino in Kaziranga and the gharial in the Chambal.

s: The red panda occurs naturally in which part of India?
x: The red panda is found in the Eastern Himalaya: Sikkim, Arunachal and Darjeeling.

s: Where in India is the saltwater crocodile found?
x: The saltwater crocodile occurs in Bhitarkanika and the Sundarbans; Chambal is the gharial's home.

s: Where in India is the Chinese pangolin naturally found?
x: The Chinese pangolin is found in the North-East; the Indian pangolin lives south of the Himalaya, not in the North-East.

s: Which of the following animal groups does NOT occur naturally in India?
x: Marsupials do not occur naturally in India.

s: In which region is the Nilgiri tahr naturally found only?
x: The Nilgiri tahr, like the lion-tailed macaque, is confined to the Western Ghats (Eravikulam).

s: Where in India is the double-humped (Bactrian) camel naturally found?
x: India's double-humped camels live only in the Nubra Valley of Ladakh.

s: The gharial is naturally associated with which river in India?
x: The gharial's main home in India is the Chambal.

s: How many countries are recognised as the world's megadiverse countries?
x: There are 17 megadiverse countries; 36 is the number of global biodiversity hotspots.

s: What are India's approximate shares of the world's land area, recorded species and population?
x: India occupies about 2.4% of the world's land area, accounts for 7–8% of recorded species and has about 18% of the world's population.

s: India contains how many of the world's 36 biodiversity hotspots?
x: India has 4 of the 36 hotspots, about 7.5% of global fauna, and over 30% of its animals are endemic.

s: Conservation International (1998) identified the 17 megadiverse countries using which criteria?
o: At least 5,000 endemic plants and a coastline bordering marine ecosystems
At least 500 endemic plants and a marine coastline
At least 5,000 endemic plants and a landlocked location
At least 5,000 animal species and no marine ecosystems
x: The criteria were at least 5,000 endemic plant species and borders with marine ecosystems.

s: In 2025, India added how many animal species to its biodiversity records?
x: India added 709 animal species in 2025 (483 new to science and 226 new records), besides 353 plant taxa.

s: Through which declaration was the Like-Minded Megadiverse Countries (LMMC) group formed in 2002?
x: The LMMC negotiating bloc was formed by the Cancun Declaration in 2002, and India is a member.

s: Where was the night frog 'Mewasingi' discovered?
x: The night frog Mewasingi was discovered in Kozhikode, Kerala (PYQ 2019). Silent Valley, Agumbe and Namdapha are other biodiversity-rich sites but are not where this frog was found.

s: In India's 2025 biodiversity additions, which State recorded the highest number of new animal species?
x: Kerala led with 98, followed by West Bengal with 76.

s: Of the 709 animal species India added in 2025, how many were new to science?
x: 483 were new to science and 226 were new records for India.

s: Who compiled India's 2025 species additions?
x: The Botanical Survey of India and Zoological Survey of India released the 2025 additions.

s: What is India's rank among the world's countries in plant richness?
x: India is 10th in plant richness, 11th in endemic higher vertebrates and 6th as a centre of crop origin.

s: Which of the following is NOT one of the 17 megadiverse countries?
x: Madagascar, Peru and Malaysia are in the list of 17 megadiverse countries; Thailand is not.

s: Over what share of India's animal species are endemic?
x: India holds about 7.5% of global fauna, and over 30% of its animals are endemic.

s: Among the world's countries, what is India's rank as a centre of origin of crops?
x: India ranks 6th in crop origin, 10th in plant richness and 11th in endemic higher vertebrates.

s: What is India's rank in the world in endemic higher vertebrates?
x: India is 10th in plant richness, 11th in endemic higher vertebrates and 6th as a centre of crop origin.

s: Who identified eight centres of origin of cultivated plants?
x: N. I. Vavilov identified eight centres of origin of cultivated plants.

s: Which of the following crop combinations is associated with the Hindustan (Indo-Burma) centre of origin?
o: Rice, sugarcane, mango, pigeon pea, brinjal, cucumber and black pepper
Wheat, barley, olive, grape and cabbage
x: The Hindustan or Indian centre is associated with rice, sugarcane, mango, pigeon pea, brinjal, cucumber and black pepper. It is also associated with many pulses and citrus.

s: What is the search in nature for commercially valuable compounds and genes called?
x: Bioprospecting is this search; biopiracy is patenting such resources or traditional knowledge without consent or compensation.

s: In which year was India's Biological Diversity Act, 2002 amended?
x: The Act was amended in 2023 and the Biological Diversity Rules, 2024 apply.

s: The Hoodia case is associated with traditional knowledge of which community?
o: The Maori people of New Zealand
The San people of southern Africa
The Toda people of southern India
The Inuit people of the Arctic
x: The appetite-suppressant use of Hoodia was based on knowledge of the San people of southern Africa, and a benefit-sharing deal followed.

s: Who set up the Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL), and when?
o: NBA and State Biodiversity Boards in 2010
x: The TKDL was set up by CSIR and AYUSH in 2001.

s: Access and Benefit Sharing (ABS) was introduced by the CBD in 1992 and made operational by which instrument?
x: ABS began with the CBD in 1992 and was made operational through the Nagoya Protocol in 2010.

s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Basmati — US patent to RiceTec, with main claims withdrawn
Neem — EPO patent involving W. R. Grace and USDA, later revoked
Turmeric — US patent on wound healing, revoked after CSIR challenge
Hoodia — patent granted to Mahyco without any benefit-sharing arrangement
x: Hoodia involved knowledge of the San people and resulted in a benefit-sharing deal. The other three pairs correctly describe the stated biopiracy cases.

s: How does the Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL) mainly prevent biopiracy?
o: Approving commercial release of GM crops
Making traditional knowledge available as prior art to patent offices
x: TKDL documents traditional knowledge so that patent offices can treat it as prior art, helping prevent wrongful patents.

s: The Borjuli wetland in Assam, a Biodiversity Heritage Site, protects Oryza rufipogon, the wild ancestor of which crop?
x: Oryza rufipogon is the ancestor of cultivated rice (Oryza sativa) and tolerates floods and salinity.

s: India’s Citrus Gene Sanctuary is located in which of the following places?
